meta.title: React Table for Large Datasets | AG Grid
meta.description: How AG Grid handles large data in React: row and column virtualisation, four row models, 100k+ rows client-side, pagination and transaction updates.
meta.demandSource: Google Ads search volume via DataForSEO (US, English, 12-month average), 2 October 2026

hero.heading: Display large datasets in a React table
hero.subHeading: AG Grid only renders the rows and columns on screen, and gives you four row models to decide how much data is sent to the browser.

shortAnswer: AG Grid handles large data in two ways. [Row and column virtualisation](./dom-virtualisation/) is on by default in every edition, including the free Community edition, so the grid only creates DOM for the cells in view plus a buffer of 10 rows above and below and 200px of columns either side. Then you choose a row model. The default [Client-Side Row Model](./row-models/) loads all rows into the browser, and the docs say it can handle 100k+ rows. When the data is too large to send, the free [Infinite Row Model](./infinite-scrolling/) loads it in blocks as the user scrolls. Enterprise adds the [Server-Side Row Model](./server-side-model/), which also groups and aggregates on the server, and the [Viewport Row Model](./viewport/) for live data streams.

items.title: Row and column virtualisation
items.body: The grid only renders the rows and columns in the visible viewport and adds or removes DOM as the user scrolls. It is on by default; `suppressRowVirtualisation` and `suppressColumnVirtualisation` turn it off.

items.title: Row buffer (rowBuffer)
items.body: Renders 10 extra rows above and below the visible rows by default so slower machines do not show blank space while scrolling. The buffer is a pixel range based on the default row height (42px in the Quartz theme). A lower value speeds up initial draws; a higher value reduces visible redraws. Columns use a separate buffer of 200px either side.

items.title: Client-Side Row Model
items.body: The default row model. All rows load in one go and sorting and filtering run in browser memory, as do grouping, pivoting and aggregation, which are Enterprise features. The docs say it handles 100k+ rows and that the browser runs out of memory before the grid has problems.

items.title: Infinite Row Model
items.body: `rowModelType='infinite'` with a datasource whose `getRows()` receives `startRow`, `endRow`, `sortModel` and `filterModel`. Rows are cached in blocks (`cacheBlockSize`, `maxBlocksInCache`, `blockLoadDebounceMillis`). The docs recommend it for large flat lists; it does not support row grouping.

items.title: Server-Side Row Model
items.body: Lazy-loads rows in blocks and loads group children only when a group is expanded, with sorting, filtering, grouping, pivoting and aggregation handed to your server. [The docs](./row-models/#when-to-use) say Enterprise users should prefer it over the Infinite Row Model.

items.title: Viewport Row Model
items.body: The grid tells your server which rows are on screen and the server sends data for those rows only, so updates reach only the users viewing them. The docs advise against it unless you need these advantages.

items.title: Massive row count (stretching)
items.body: Browsers cap the height of a div (32,000,000px on Chrome v118 per the docs, about 320,000 rows at 100px each). Beyond that the grid offsets row positions as you scroll, so scrolling appears faster in proportion to the extra space needed.

items.title: Pagination
items.body: `pagination=true` replaces vertical scrolling with pages and works with all four row models. `paginationAutoPageSize` fits as many rows per page as the grid height allows.

items.title: Transaction updates
items.body: `applyTransaction()` adds, removes and updates specific rows instead of replacing all row data; with `getRowId` rows are matched by ID, which the docs describe as faster than object references for large datasets. `applyTransactionAsync()` batches updates, applied after 50ms by default. These are Client-Side Row Model APIs; the Server-Side Row Model has `applyServerSideTransaction()` and `applyServerSideTransactionAsync()` (Enterprise).

items.title: Scrolling performance options
items.body: The docs suggest testing without custom cell renderers, using value getters or formatters instead where possible, deferring slow renderers with `deferRender: true`, avoiding auto row height, and setting `suppressRowHoverHighlight=true`.

howTo.heading: How to handle large datasets in a React table

steps.title: Start with the default row model and a fixed height
steps.body: Load your rows into `rowData` and give the grid container a set height. Virtualisation needs a known height; the grid caps rendering at 500 rows to protect against containers that grow to fit every row.

steps.title: Profile, then tune rendering
steps.body: Compare your grid with the AG Grid performance demo at the same size. Remove custom cell renderers to see if they are the cost, use `valueFormatter` instead where possible, mark slow renderers with `cellRendererParams: { deferRender: true }`, and adjust `rowBuffer`.

steps.title: Load in blocks when the data is too big to send
steps.body: Set `rowModelType='infinite'` and a datasource whose `getRows(params)` fetches `params.startRow` to `params.endRow`, sorted on the server by `params.sortModel`, and calls `params.successCallback(rows, lastRow)`. With Enterprise, use `rowModelType='serverSide'` instead to keep grouping and aggregation on the server.

steps.title: Update rows with transactions
steps.body: With the default row model, use `api.applyTransaction({ add, update, remove })` with `getRowId` rather than replacing `rowData`. For many small updates in quick succession, `applyTransactionAsync()` batches them. With the Server-Side Row Model, use `api.applyServerSideTransaction()`.

steps.title: Choose scrolling or pagination
steps.body: Past the browser's maximum div height the grid stretches rows and scrolling feels faster. If that does not suit your users, the docs suggest showing fewer rows or turning on `pagination`.

howTo.outro: See the [performance demo](/example/): pick a data size up to 100,000 rows while scrolling, sorting and filtering, with React, JavaScript, Angular and Vue source on GitHub.

faq.question: How many rows can AG Grid handle in React?
faq.answer: There is no fixed row limit in the grid. The row models guide says the default Client-Side Row Model can handle 100k+ rows and that the browser runs out of memory first. Separately, browsers cap div height, so past roughly 320,000 rows at 100px each on Chrome v118 the grid stretches rows, so scrolling appears faster.

faq.question: Does AG Grid virtualise rows and columns?
faq.answer: Yes, both, by default and in the free Community edition. Only the visible rows and columns are in the DOM, plus a 10-row buffer above and below and a 200px column buffer either side.

faq.question: Which row model should I use for large data?
faq.answer: The docs' rule of thumb: use the Client-Side Row Model if you can load all data into the browser. If not, use the Infinite Row Model in Community or the Server-Side Row Model in Enterprise to load data in blocks. Use the Viewport Row Model only if you need the server to know exactly which rows each user is viewing.

faq.question: Is there a React table large data example?
faq.answer: Yes. The [AG Grid performance demo](/example/) renders up to 100,000 rows, or 10,000 rows by 100 columns, and lets you change the size while you scroll, sort and filter. The React source is on GitHub, along with JavaScript, Angular and Vue versions.

faq.question: Can a large table be editable?
faq.answer: Yes. Cell editors work with all four row models. On the Client-Side and Server-Side Row Models you can also push changes from the server with transactions.

faq.question: Does the Quick Filter work on large server-side data?
faq.answer: No. The Quick Filter is supported only on the Client-Side Row Model. With the other row models you implement equivalent filtering on your server; the Infinite and Server-Side Row Models send column filter models with each request.

proseClaims.claim: There is no fixed limit to the number of rows the grid can display.
The grid only renders the rows and columns in the visible viewport, adding and removing DOM as the user scrolls; suppressRowVirtualisation and suppressColumnVirtualisation turn this off.
By default the grid renders 10 rows above and 10 rows below the visible rows; rowBuffer changes this.
The row buffer is a pixel range of rowBuffer multiplied by the default row height, which is 42px in the Quartz theme.
The grid also renders columns within 200px either side of the visible set.
The grid renders a maximum of 500 rows as a safety measure; suppressMaxRenderedRowRestriction removes the limit.
A lower rowBuffer makes initial draws faster and a higher one reduces visible redraws when scrolling.
The Client-Side Row Model is the default, loads all data in one go and can handle 100k+ rows, with the browser running out of memory before the grid has problems.
Community users should use the Infinite Row Model to load data in blocks; Enterprise users should prefer the Server-Side Row Model over it.
The Infinite Row Model is for large, flat lists and does not support grouping or aggregation.
The Infinite Row Model datasource getRows() receives startRow, endRow, sortModel and filterModel, and blocks are configured with cacheBlockSize, maxBlocksInCache and blockLoadDebounceMillis.
With the Infinite Row Model the grid cannot sort or filter rows itself, so sorting and filtering must be done on the server.
The Server-Side Row Model is an Enterprise feature that lazy-loads rows in blocks and loads group children when a group is expanded, with server-side grouping, pivoting and aggregation.
The Viewport Row Model is an Enterprise feature in which the server sends data only for the rows on screen, and the docs advise against it unless you need its advantages.
The Quick Filter is only supported with the Client-Side Row Model.
Cell editors work with all four row models; transactions work with the Client-Side and Server-Side Row Models.
On Chrome v118 the maximum div height was 32,000,000px, about 320,000 rows at 100px, and beyond that the grid stretches rows so scrolling appears faster.
Pagination works with all row models, and paginationAutoPageSize fits as many rows per page as the grid height allows.
Transactions matched by getRowId are faster than matching by object reference, which is slow for large datasets.
applyTransactionAsync() batches transactions and applies them after 50ms by default (asyncTransactionWaitMillis).
Server-Side Row Model transactions are an Enterprise feature.

For scrolling performance the docs suggest testing without cell renderers, using value getters or formatters instead, deferring slow renderers with deferRender, avoiding auto row height and setting suppressRowHoverHighlight.
The performance demo offers sizes from 100 to 100,000 rows, including 10,000 rows by 100 columns, with source for JavaScript, React, Angular and Vue on GitHub.
